rationale: The paper is an in-scope small-molecule homogeneous organic reaction study. The authors performed non-routine DFT calculations directly on methanethiolate addition to three electron-deficient [3]dendralene substrates and reported relative Gibbs free energies and selected barriers for anionic intermediates, protonated products, and cyclization pathways. The public question is bounded to the authors' computed reaction phenomenon and does not require reproducing a named author mechanism. Public inputs identify only the substrates, computational model, and conditions; the author-computed selectivity outcomes remain private references.

ABSTRACT: Electron-deficient dendralenes, bearing enone substructures and possessing an unfavorable disposition of like charges at the neighboring carbons, undergo nucleophilic 1,4-addition (Michael) or 1,6-addition (anti-Michael). Diverse products are obtained, including those of simple addition as well as cyclic and ortho-fused systems arising via multistep sequences, depending on the structure of the substrate and the nature of the nucleophile. Attack of a hydride at an enone fragment triggers the formation of multisubstituted pyranones and furans; furan formation was also initiated by thiolates. A notable exception is the derivative with a five-membered cyclic enone, which prefers simple additions followed by the reshufling of the double bonds for both H<sup>−</sup> and RS<sup>−</sup> nucleophiles. By contrast, the latter enone is the only one that

can react with stabilized C-nucleophiles, yielding bicyclic compounds. Domino cyclizations can also be induced by the enolization of the enone with DBU, giving mostly polysubstituted furans. However, the dendralene with a five-membered cyclic enone and its analogue with a six-membered ring behave diferently: The former gives a mixture, while the latter prefers the formation of an isocoumarin derivative, which is driven by aromatization. DFT calculations have shown that the additions of thiolates are mostly governed by the thermodynamic stability of possible products arising from complex equilibrium processes.

scientific_question: For the three electron-deficient [3]dendralene substrates bearing (i) a cyclopentenone appendage, (ii) a cyclohexenone appendage, and (iii) a phenylsulfonyl appendage, how does methanethiolate addition distribute among the accessible conjugated electrophilic sites under standard solution conditions, and which simple-addition or cyclized products are thermodynamically favored after protonation? Compare the relevant anionic addition intermediates and protonated products for these three substrates without assuming a common site-selectivity rule.
computation_relevance: The authors explicitly selected thiolate addition because it showed variable experimental behavior and modeled reactions of the cyclopentenone, cyclohexenone, and phenylsulfonyl dendralenes with methanethiolate. They reported DFT Gibbs free energies for anionic intermediates, protonated products, and selected cyclization barriers, and used these results to rationalize why the cyclopentenone substrate gives a simple addition product, the cyclohexenone substrate gives a cyclized furan product, and the phenylsulfonyl substrate gives an alpha-site addition product.

reference_limitations: The authors used methanethiolate as a model for ethanethiolate/2-mercaptoethanol experiments, so quantitative comparison to experimental thiolate reactions is approximate.
The authors report that some product free-energy differences for the cyclopentenone substrate are within typical DFT error and that the most stable product varied across DFT methods.
The reported calculations use implicit chloroform solvation and standard-state corrections; they do not include explicit solvent, counterions, or full experimental workup effects.

The authors state that thiolate attacks generally have negligible barriers and that product thermodynamics mostly govern outcomes, but exact uncertainty ranges for all barriers and energies are not reported.
The computational references are conditional on the authors' selected stationary points and model systems; they should not be treated as exhaustive proof of all possible pathways.
